We investigate the approximation of a parabolic stochastic optimal control problem where the diffusion coefficient contains the control parameter. Due to the nonlinearity and potential lack of smoothness in the associated stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE), direct finite element approximation proves unfeasible. To overcome this, we first prove a new monotonicity property of the fully discrete system, enabling approximation via a finite element method in the time-discretized setting. This is followed by an analysis of the error associated with the Monte-Carlo method. The findings in this paper extend earlier work [8] to cases involving less smooth data.

Stochastic optimal control constitutes a central area of research and application in mathematical finance. A key challenge in solving such problems is handling the optimal control expression, which typically involves an inverse Monte-Carlo integration that lacks a closed-form solution. To address this, Peng and Zhou [8] proposed a two-step approximation: first, approximating the stochastic maximal coupling problem, and second, applying the Monte-Carlo method to the resulting decoupled system of SPDEs. The primary contribution of this paper is to enhance the convergence rate of the Monte-Carlo approximation found in [8]. The improvement is achieved by employing a mixed finite element method for the state equation and a careful error analysis of the resulting system. As a contribution to numerical analysis for mathematical finance, this work further establishes the convergence of the approximate optimal control problem, specifically proving the existence of a discrete version of the HJB equation and its connection to the original problem.

This paper extends the findings of [6] to scenarios where the data lacks smoothness. The proof strategy relies on establishing a monotonicity property of the fully discrete system. The main contributions of this study are an error analysis for the two-step approximation method and the demonstration of its convergence.

In a prior work, the author proved the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution for a specific parabolic SPDE. This paper builds on that result to analyze a variational inequality linked to the SPDE. The proof for the inequality follows a standard approach, relying on the previously established weak solution. ray anisotropies observed by the Pierre Auger Observatory for energies exceeding 4 EeV. While a dipolar modulation in right ascension at energies above 8 EeV was previously identified as the most prominent signal within the [4,8] EeV and $E\geq 8$ EeV bins, we further investigate the highest-energy range by dividing it into three distinct intervals. Our results indicate that the dipole amplitude grows with energy above 4 EeV, a trend well-described by a power law with an index of $\beta=0.79\pm 0.19$. The dipole directions remain consistent with an extragalactic origin across all examined energies. Furthermore, our estimation of quadrupolar components reveals no statistical significance. Finally, we contextualize these findings against various models predicting the distribution of ultrahigh-energy sources and cosmic magnetic fields. The observed dipole amplitudes are most compatible with a population of superluminous sources located at intermediate distances. This conclusion remains robust even when incorporating the recently identified quadrupole signal or when source distributions are allowed to evolve with energy. Our discoveries do not support either completely random source distributions or a sky configuration consisting of only a few sources at great distances. Furthermore, the superluminous source scenario at intermediate ranges successfully accounts for the Amagnetic Limit reported by the Auger-CTA collaboration. The determined power-law index offers quantitative support for recent spectral analyses and could be effectively interpreted if the deflection of ultrahigh-energy magnetic particles becomes dominant before the knee of the galactic halo's magnetic field power spectrum. This implies a knee angular scale of approximately $10^{-3}$ rad, regardless of the specific functional form of the spectrum. We also address the implications of our results for the primordial magnetic field. Supplementary findings supporting the main conclusions are discussed based on simulated data. Supplementary Information is referenced throughout the manuscript. The findings presented in this paper are supported by the results found in this paper.

Ultrasoud-assisted telescopic spraying utilizes a spray tip sonotrode to generate intense ultrasonic vibrations within the coating material, thereby enhancing the cleaning, wetting, and flushing effects during the removal of molten metal skin from reinforcing steel. This study employs a 3D high-speed camera to capture the dynamics of an ultrasonic droplet impacting a horizontal water surface at atmospheric pressure. Utilizing continuum mechanics simulations that incorporate an acoustic body force term derived from holographic measurements, we replicate the experimental observations.

Gbit/s optical on-off keying (OOK) system operating over 18.8 km of uncompensated submarine fiber in the South China Sea. The chromatic dispersion inherent in this cable length creates four spectral nulls within the 36 GHz bandwidth of the OOK signal, posing a significant barrier to achieving acceptable bit-error-rate (BER) performance. While a decision feedback equalizer (DFE) can effectively address these spectral nulls, it suffers from burst-error propagation caused by signal instability in the harsh submarine environment. Although a weighted DFE (WDFE) helps mitigate burst-error propagation, it fails to fully compensate for spectral nulls because it relies on only a subset of directly decided feedback symbols. Proposed joint decision-feedback equalizers (JDFE) successfully overcome these limitations, delivering superior BER performance compared to a standard DFE. Unlike the conventional DFE, which requires approximately 1.25 GHz of optical bandwidth to avoid spectral nulls, the WDFE and especially the JDFE can effectively utilize the full ~36 GHz dispersion tolerance of the OOK signal. Consequently, the 36 GHz bandwidth of the carrier signal was compressed to 1.25 GHz using a surface acoustic wave filter; this narrow bandwidth, combined with the advanced equalization techniques, enabled the successful transmission of 72 Gbit/s over the specified distance. Finally, the transmission quality of the carrier was assessed using the Q factor and the BER methods. This research provides critical insights into overcoming the spectral nulls generated by chromatic dispersion in wide-bandwidth OOK carriers, validating the feasibility of JDFE for next-generation wide-bandwidth optical transmission systems. Additionally, the achieved Q factor of 8.05 supports the potential for improving transmission quality further through forward error correction (FEC). The proposed joint equalization scheme is also expected to be relevant for optimizing energy efficiency in wide-bandwidth optical transmission. Although the current record for wide-bandwidth OOK transmission is 111.2 Gbit/s over 50 km of uncompensated fiber without FEC, the system demonstrated here—utilizing a more efficient 72 Gbit/s modulation format and verified without FEC—successfully overcame the spectral nulls imposed by chromatic dispersion over a significantly longer distance of 188 km of uncompensated submarine fiber. This was achieved through the application of a weighted decision-feedback equalizer (WDFE) and the novel decision-feedback equalizer (NDFE).

highly effective deep learning architectures for processing time-series data, yet optimizing their core time-dilated convolution mechanism often demands significant experimentation. We introduce an automatic dilation optimizer that reframes this challenge as weight pruning along the time axis, enabling the simultaneous learning of dilation factors and network weights within a single training phase. This approach achieves up to a 7.4x reduction in model size and a 3x decrease in inference latency on real System-on-Chip (SoC) hardware, all without sacrificing accuracy compared to non-dilated networks. Furthermore, our method generates a diverse collection of Pareto-optimal TCNs from a single initial model, surpassing manually designed solutions in both efficiency and performance. Essential to our approach are two innovations: (1) a novel auxiliary convolution layer that permits the simultaneous learning of filter dimensions and dilation rates, and (2) an adaptive share strategy for shared weights within symmetric dilated convolutions, which minimizes the increase in the number of learnable parameters. Experimental results confirm that our automatically optimized TCNs exceed the efficiency of hand-tuned models by 5% to 26% in terms of model size, memory usage, and inference latency, while maintaining equivalent accuracy. The source code is available at https://github.com/zeyadem/dilation-optimizer.
Efficient processing of high-dimensional time series is crucial for deploying machine learning models on resource-constrained devices. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely used for this purpose, but manually designing them with appropriate dilation factors to balance accuracy and efficiency remains challenging. We present a learning-based method for automatically optimizing the time-dilated convolution operation in fully dilated CNNs. This allows the simultaneous learning of filter sizes and dilation factors alongside network weights. By leveraging the weight-sharing structure of fully convolved layers, we place a lower bound on the network's parameter count, ensuring that optimized networks are at least as parameter-efficient as any manually designed counterpart. We provide theoretical justification for why this problem is tractable and interesting, and we address the computational challenges of learning dilation factors, which is non-trivial due to the discrete nature of the operation. Extensive experiments on various CNNs across different input sizes demonstrate that our method can automatically learn both dilation factors and filter dimensions to maintain equivalent accuracy with reduced model size, or to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy without increasing size. This results in a 18x reduction in model size and a 6x reduction in inference latency on SoC hardware without any compromise in accuracy. The code can be accessed at

These analyses cover various centralities in Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV using the ALICE detector at the LHC. Sensitivity studies suggest that future measurements of these fluctuations in smaller-centralities with higher statistics could significantly constrain the $\eta/s$ of the QGP. We report the first determination of the elliptic flow coefficient $U\{ell\}$ for charged particles using the large acceptance of the ALICE detector at the LHC. This is achieved through the multi--particle method, which exploits the azimuthal anisotropy in the distribution of relative angles between particles. The measured $U\{ell\}$ for charged particles rises with transverse momentum for $p_{\rm T}\lesssim 8$ GeV/$c$. When normalized by the number of participating pairs, $U\{ell\}$ for charged particles for mid--central collisions shows little dependence on energy for $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The derived single--particle elliptic flow coefficient for charged particles is consistent with, and can be derived from, the $U\{ell\}$ values for negatively charged kaons, pions, and kaons. These findings provide new insights into particle production and the evolution of the quark--gluon plasma.

Specifically, the ALBA algorithm, which is parametric for each (D)LE, efficiently determines the first-order correspondents of (D)LE-inductive formulas. We introduce an algorithm that utilizes ALBA's rules and algebraic framework to reverse its steps within the DLE context, thereby effectively deriving an inductive formula from its given first-order correspondent. When applied to (D)LEs, this method is particularly valuable for generating inductive formulas given their first-order correspondents. Furthermore, we examine its implications for 2-leader ALBA and its extensions, including ALBA+ and ALBA+, as well as ALBA for predicate logic. Order-theoretic inductivity serves as the cornerstone for ALBA algorithm design; similarly, we demonstrate how to investigate DLE-inductivity from its first-order perspective and apply it across various (D)LEs. This research provides a comprehensive framework for exploring ALBA and its extensions, facilitating a holistic investigation of any specific (D)LE inductivity condition. In a related development, a colleague recently proved that every DLE is essentially equivalent to a distributive lattice expansion, suggesting a broader framework for examining ALBA algorithms across all lattice expansions. At its core, this methodology relies on the translation of classical first-order formulas into propositional DLEs via the short ALBA test. We propose a similar approach to translate first-order DLEs into propositional ones and utilize it to analyze the ALBA test for first-order DLEs. Our investigations into ALBA algorithm extensions for (D)LEs and first-order DLEs reveal a striking simplicity and elegance in the entire process. These methods not only facilitate a comprehensive study of ALBA extensions for (D)LEs and first-order DLEs but also provide an accessible and effective means for investigating any specific DLE in detail. In conclusion, the findings presented in and are interconnected through a shared underlying framework. The research avenues explored in these works will be further extended in my upcoming PhD thesis.

While the conventional stance holds that table instances must adhere to all imposed functional dependencies, it is equally significant to formulate theories for handling instances that violate certain dependencies. Concerning missing values, we do not presuppose their existence; rather, a missing value is considered to exist only if it can be inferred from the table's functional dependencies.

We present a formal framework where each table tuple is assigned one of four truth values: true, false, inconsistent, or unknown. We demonstrate that this framework facilitates the study of critical issues such as consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality metrics, among others. However, this work primarily concentrates on consistent query answering, a problem that has garnered significant attention over recent decades.

The paper's main contributions are as follows: (a) we introduce a novel approach for addressing inconsistencies in tables with nulls and functional dependencies; (b) we provide the definition and formalization of the consistent query answering problem within this context; and (c) we examine several simple cases to illustrate the application of consistent query answering.

The paper is structured into four additional sections plus this introduction. Section Section:Background offers some background information, and Section Section:Preliminaries defines the problem of consistent query answering and establishes several of its fundamental properties. The findings from Section Section:Preliminaries, alongside the results from Section Section:Consistent Query Answering Properties, constitute the paper's core contributions.

AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Under mild conditions, we establish the asymptotic properties of the TV-PARX model, proving that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) produces parameter estimates that are both strongly consistent and asymptotically normal. Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess finite-sample performance and forecasting precision. Furthermore, the practical value of the TV-PARX model's time-varying specification is illustrated through an analysis of daily new COVID-19 infections in Italy and corporate defaults in the United States. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of its findings and suggestions for future research directions. This work extends the TVARX framework to Poisson distributions and provides an accessible reference for implementing time-varying parameter autoregressive models for count data. The corresponding Python code is available at https://github.com/riccardofanenni/TV-POISSON.

The primary contribution of this paper is to generalize the time-varying parameter ARX (TVARX) model to accommodate univariate count time series, specifically those following a Poisson distribution.

We present a time-varying parameter autoregressive with exogenous variables (ARX) model suitable for univariate count time series that exhibit non-constant variance and time-dependent variance. The proposed model parameters are estimated using a quasi-maximum likelihood (QML) approach, with their asymptotic properties examined. Additionally, a LASSO penalty is incorporated to enhance the model's forecasting capabilities. A simulation study and an empirical analysis are conducted to evaluate in-sample and out-of-sample forecasting performance. These results indicate that the proposed time-series model is effective in producing reliable forecasts for count data. This model can be applied to forecast various economic and financial indicators, such as monthly employment counts in the US, daily infections in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, and bond issuances.

a novel object representation that encodes points and relative poses between an object and a target (like a robot gripper or hanging rack) using category-level descriptors. Designed for object manipulation, this approach enables the repetition of a demonstrated task on new instances within the same category by optimizing for a pose whose descriptor matches the observed demonstration. NDFs are trained in a self-supervised manner through a 3D auto-encoding process that avoids the need for expert-labeled keypoints. Additionally, their SE(3)-equivariant nature ensures robust generalization across all 3D translations and rotations. We address multi-view pose estimation for 3D objects with known models, extending previously separate tasks of keypoint detection and relative pose estimation into a single, mutually supportive framework. This allows for the determination of any 6-DoF pose from 3 or more views, even when only a single 2-D silhouette is visible per object. We introduce 3-DoF Keypose Maps, which represent simultaneously valid keypoints and relative poses (up to translation) for a object and a model, respectively. These maps are encoded by a neural field trained via 3D interpolation to generalize across object instances, orientations, and camera poses. Training relies on a small dataset of a few object instances, each with a limited number of keypoints and silhouettes captured from a few views. To handle ambiguous map values, we propose a stochastic sampling strategy that selects a consistent local fragment of the map. Experiments show that our method outperforms keypose networks (Wu et al., 2019) for pose estimation when only 2 or 3 views are visible and achieves competitive results against other state-of-the-art solutions.

stars within the high-metallicity globular cluster Tononzintla~2 (Ton~2), utilizing high-resolution near-infrared spectra from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment II (APOGEE-2) survey, specifically as part of the bulge Cluster APOgee Survey. Our study examines chemical abundances across various elemental groups—including light, odd-Z, $\alpha$, Fe-peak, and neutron-capture elements—based on high signal-to-noise spectra of seven giant members. The resulting mean cluster metallicity is determined to be [Fe/H]$=-0.70\pm0.05$, showing no signs of intrinsic metallicity dispersion. Ton~2 displays a standard $\alpha$-enrichment pattern consistent with other high-metallicity Galactic globular clusters, mirroring trends observed in 47~Tucanae and NGC~6380. However, we detect a significant spread in nitrogen abundance ($>0.87$ dex) and a substantial population of nitrogen-enriched stars. Considering Ton~2's relatively high metallicity, these nitrogen levels far exceed typical Galactic averages, confirming the prevalence of the multiple-population phenomenon; the cluster also hosts stars with low, first-generation nitrogen abundances. Additionally, we identify a [Ce/Fe] abundance spread in Ton~2 that correlates with nitrogen enhancement, suggesting that \textit{s}-process enrichment was likely driven by the pulsational thermal driving (PTD) of an intermediate-mass star. Finally, the spectral data from Ton~2 will aid in discerning the stellar origins of distinct groups in globular clusters and understanding their formation histories. The findings from Ton~2 are comparable to previous studies of similar mass and metallicity, such as NGC~6380 and 47~Tuc, yet they offer unique insights into multiple-population characteristics in high-metallicity clusters. To achieve these abundance measurements, approximately 100 tons of APOGEE-2 observations were required, a effort that will not be sustainable given the limited number of available IRD cameras on the Keck II telescope. Consequently, the chemical evolution models predicted to explain these abundances will need to incorporate 1D stellar evolutionary tracks featuring heterogeneous mixing processes, the ability to simulate multiple-populations, and an understanding of the downsides of convection overshoot and merger timescales.

Existing literature is generally categorized into two approaches based on the use of intermediate cues: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter, CNNs regress intermediate features like 3D coordinates, semantic keypoints, or virtual control points in the first stage, with object pose subsequently determined through correspondence constraints derived from these cues. Despite certain modeling constraints, Bond-Based Peridynamics (BB-PD) remains a popular choice for numerical simulations, largely due to its ease of implementation, physical clarity, and stability. Peridynamics offers a framework for investigating the initiation and progression of cracks and other discontinuities within solid materials. Bond-Based Peridynamics (BB-PD) serves as a primary method for solving these problems, relying on integral kernels that define the strength of bonds between material points. This work introduces two new peridynamic kernel functions, the Linear Tensile and the Linear Elastic-Kirchhoff (ELK) kernels. These kernels are applied to simulate crack propagation in a rock-like material, with the ELK kernel specifically demonstrating the formation of process zone characteristics such as crack arrest and branching. The findings indicate that the ELK kernel more accurately replicates experimental process zone behaviors, whereas a purely elastic-kirchhoff kernel fails to capture these effects. Furthermore, the accuracy of the simulation is shown to depend on the size of the horizon; smaller horizons require finer mesh resolutions to achieve satisfactory results. In conclusion, the introduced kernels provide effective mechanisms for modeling material failure and can be adapted for additional complex scenarios. Context: Gravitational wave (GW) signals from merging binary black holes (BBHs) are influenced not only by the final spin configuration but also by the system's evolution within its surroundings. While most BBHs are expected to reside in stellar-mass or planetary-mass dark matter (DM) environments, the impact of this interaction on the inspiral phase remains unclear. This research analyzes the quasi-stationary evolution of a circular, quasi-circular, and wandering BBH in a DM halo containing wave dark matter (WDM), modeled as a superposition of coherent complex scalar fields. This approach differs from previous studies because it does not rely on superimposing a circular BBH onto a $\psi$-soliton. Results show that for WDM with a mass $m_\psi < 0.15 \, {\rm eV}$, the BBH experiences a quasi-stationary evolution where the scalar field builds up to a stationary state after several orbital periods. In contrast, WDM with $m_\psi \gtrsim 0.15 \, {\rm eV}$ leads to immediate field dispersion. Simply superimposing a circular BBH onto the stationary state creates an artificial eccentricity caused by matter backreaction, an artifact of the initialization. To extract gravitational wave waveforms from WDM around a wandering BBH, it is essential to define a realistic and computationally efficient initial condition scheme where the field reaches a stationary state

The edges are hinged at their outer vertices, while the central vertex allows for both translation and rotation; the rotational motion is influenced by a combination of elastic and frictional forces. We provide comprehensive findings regarding the asymptotic distribution and structure of the spectrum for the linear operator linked to the abstract spectral problem within a Hilbert space. Finally, the specific link between Riesz bases and exponential stability is illustrated by showing that integrating derivative terms of the transverse displacements into the operator yields an unconditional Riesz basis and consequently, exponential stability. This model defines a multilayer network as a collection of multiple edge-weighted, potentially directed graphs sharing the same set of nodes, where each graph constitutes a layer and no edges connect nodes across different layers. Similar to standard eigenvector centrality, a node's importance in a specific layer is derived from the weighted sum of its neighbors' importance within that same layer. However, unlike the standard approach, our framework allows the adjacency relationships and the importance values of neighboring nodes to originate from different layers. Crucially, this capability is only partially addressed by current multilayer eigenvector centrality frameworks, which typically rely on inter-layer edges to model such dependencies. In our proposed model, constrained, layer-specific eigenvector centrality scores are determined by a system comprising independent eigenvalue problems and dependent pseudo-eigenvalue problems, which can be solved efficiently through an interleaved power iteration algorithm. We demonstrate that the central component of our approach—calculating importance alongside dependencies—also applies to other centrality metrics, such as betweenness and closeness centrality. Furthermore, we present a Python implementation of our method, which is released under a permissive license to facilitate future extensions. Finally, we illustrate the practical application of our model in assessing the removal of a single node or an entire layer from a multilayer network. ### 1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) excels in artificial settings but often struggles when deployed outside controlled domains. As a data-efficient method relying on environmental interactions for supervision, RL in RL becomes vulnerable when adversaries gain access to observe executions and inject corrupting noise into rewards and/or transitions. Understanding the feasibility, sample complexity, and reliability of RL learning amidst such corruption is crucial, particularly given the ease with which attacks can be executed. Consequently, developing robust RL algorithms resistant to these attacks is both a significant challenge and a priority.

Under the broad assumption that an attacker possesses full observational power and can modify both rewards and transitions up to a small fraction $\epsilon$ of the total episode count, Li and Tompson~\cite{li2019attacks} proved the impossibility of achieving any non-trivial regret bound. Specifically, their lower bound indicates that the expected return cannot exceed the optimal policy's value by more than $O(\epsilon)$, implying that only a weakly suboptimal policy is guaranteed when either rewards or transitions are corrupted.

Current work presents an automated LTO system featuring a reduced-order surrogate for the geological model, which matches the accuracy of traditional methods but is $10^4$ to $10^5$ times faster, enabling the optimization of 1 to 100 wells within minutes. The integration of this automated system into a complete LTO workflow opens multiple research avenues, including improving the objective function through better data assimilation, applying multi-objective optimization to balance hydrocarbon recovery with drilling costs, and conducting multi-disciplinary optimizations that account for hydrogeological and structural constraints. Ultimately, the success of this approach relies on the continuous automation and refinement of the geological model surrogate and the identified key performance indicators.

Recent years have seen significant advances in both the accuracy and speed of methods for hydrocarbon reservoir simulation and optimization. However, these achievements have typically been isolated, leaving a gap in applying a comprehensive solution to the specific challenges of local target exploration. This report reviews the current landscape of techniques for data-assisted geological modeling, proxy-based modeling, simulation, and optimization. It highlights where the field stands today, identifies the most pressing research questions, and outlines an integrated framework for their application. This report was prepared to guide a multi-year, multi-national project (H2020 GeoOptLTO) dedicated to exploring this topic in depth.

Finding optimal well locations and associated control settings to maximize a specific objective function is vital in the exploration phase of reservoir management. Due to the intricate data involved and the extensive range of possible well positions, modern decision-making relies on surrogate-based Bayesian optimization. This report examines the entire process of locating a well from the seabed to the reservoir, examining every step that could potentially influence the final decision during the well-logging phase. The scope of the problem is defined by a case study of the initial well location for a small cluster of approximately 10 wells, drawn from actual industrial experiences. Nested NER, a specific subset of NER, involves named entities that are contained within one another. However, many prior studies on nested NER utilize linear structures to model entities that inherently possess a hierarchical organization. To resolve this discrepancy, this work treats all nested entities within a sentence as a unified structure and introduces a hierarchical attention mechanism to facilitate effective NER performance. Furthermore, to enhance the model's capacity to extract nested entities, we treat them as sequences and employ a recursive network to construct a custom feature representation for these entities. To prevent over-smoothing during recursion, we incorporate residual connections into our proposed model. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on two recognized nested NER datasets. Additionally, the constructed feature representation for nested entities demonstrates superior quality, as evidenced by its success in a information extraction task. This finding underscores the significance of nested entities for extracting repeated information and provides evidence that our model can effectively learn to perform NER on such entities. Introduction
Named entity recognition (NER) is a critical task for various downstream applications including knowledge extraction, question answering, and document summarization. Recent advances indicate that NER encompasses a diverse range of subtasks, such as multi-label and hierarchical (nested) NER. Nested NER involves identifying entities that contain one another, a task that proves particularly challenging due to its difficulty, limited resources, and scarce research attention. To overcome these obstacles, this paper addresses the problem from a theoretical perspective. Specifically, existing methods typically handle nested entities containing the same type of information by linearly stacking their mentions, which can lead to ambiguity and misclassification. To mitigate this issue, we address three key questions: 1) How can we effectively represent nested entities that share identical information? 2) Can we establish an entity space to perform NER more efficiently? and 3) What impact does nested entity information sharing have on feature representation and NER performance? Addressing these questions yields three contributions to theoretical feature representation, entity space construction, and performance analysis, respectively. Our experimental results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on two standard nested NER datasets. The successful feature representation of nested entities under our model also validates its potential for downstream tasks like information extraction. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate and compare energy consumption across various wireless sensor network (WSN) protocols. Our analysis covers the expected energy received (EEE), payload energy consumption (PEC), and total energy consumption (EC) for protocols including IEEE 802.15.4, ZigBee, IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPAN), Cross-state routing for lossy networks (XMAC/XTP), directed IWAN mac (DWMAC), and the wireless sensor network protocol (WSNP). Findings indicate that the energy consumption of these protocols fluctuates based on transmission distance and data packet sizes. Specifically, protocols operating with shorter communication ranges exhibit lower energy consumption. Furthermore, we present a graph illustrating these findings, which can guide researchers in selecting the most appropriate protocol for specific application requirements. It is hoped that this analysis will aid in developing more energy-efficient wireless communication protocols and that the conclusions drawn can support correct protocol selection within smart home applications. Finally, the research shows that the energy consumption of the selected protocols varies depending on the number of active nodes.

We hypothesized that this phenomenon significantly influences online misinformation dissemination because, despite their global potential, digital interactions are inherently localized, with interaction likelihood dropping sharply as distance increases. Analyzing over 8 million Reddit comments containing news links from January 2016 to December 2019, we discovered that Reddit does not function as a "hype machine" for misinformation as other platforms do; instead, it operates as a supply-and-demand system. Specifically, the volume of misinformation news scaled linearly with the population of each state (scaling exponent $\beta=1$, $R^2 = 0.95$). Moreover, variations from this universal trend were best predicted by state-level personality and cultural attributes ($R^2 = \{0.12, 0.39\}$), rather than socioeconomic factors ($R^2 = \{0.15, 0.29\}$) or political characteristics ($R^2 = \{0.06, 0.21\}$). We observed that states with residents exhibiting lower conscientiousness and cultures characterized by loose norms (low cultural tightness) experienced higher-than-expected circulation of all news and fact-checked fake news, while those with highly conscientious individuals and tight cultures saw lower-than-expected circulation. Finally, we proposed that the need for cognitive dissonance reduction drives the spread of fake news in "The Big Sort," whereas the availability heuristic supports its spread in states with low conscientiousness and loose norms. Consequently, the geographic spread of misinformation is not random but shaped by the cultural and personality profiles of local populations. Consequently, combating misinformation requires addressing offline cultural differences alongside online mechanisms and digital literacy. Furthermore, we contend that The Big Sort exacerbates political polarization by driving the digital migration of individuals to like-minded locations, thereby creating insulated echo chambers that amplify existing views.

Deploying accurate detection systems is essential for supporting human experts across various sectors of modern digital society; however, because these systems exert significant normative influence, understanding their inner workings must be considered a fundamental human right. Conceptually, HALFADO builds upon a classic classification learning algorithm, retaining its theoretical strengths while functioning in a semi-supervised manner that merges human and computational intelligence. Practically, it surpasses traditional expert systems by unifying and enhancing their capabilities into a single global detector. We demonstrate HALFADO's effectiveness in two demanding scenarios: detecting hate speech in social media text streams and identifying fraudulent transactions within financial data for a Transaction Monitoring System (TMS). This work shows that contrary to common assumptions, sophisticated machine learning methods do not necessarily demand immense computational resources or costly annotation efforts. Instead, methods like HALFADO can deliver superior performance by seamlessly integrating human expertise with computational intelligence. By facilitating such intelligent system deployments, this approach not only deepens our understanding of automated detection mechanisms but also ensures they align with human intent and values. Consequently, HALFADO serves as an exemplary tool for creating high-performing, transparent, and equitable deployments of automated detection systems. Deploying systems like HALFADO is critical for ensuring digital societies function in a safe, secure, fair, inclusive, and sustainable manner. Ultimately, initiatives such as HALFADO are a cornerstone of Building Digital Trust within the European Union's Digital Decade framework. In all deployment contexts, practitioners should strive for solutions characterized by mutual understanding between humans and machines, transparency, and efficiency. We hope that HALFADO inspires future research into hybrid systems for sensitive detection tasks and acts as a foundational step toward developing certifications for automated suspicious event detection. The source code for HALFADO is available at code.github.com/HalfADO.

Although demonstrations offer a natural method for teaching robots, relying solely on movement trajectories fails to incorporate other modalities, such as audio cues from human instructors. To harness these audio signals effectively, it is essential to first identify the specific information they convey. This study characterizes the audio generated by human teachers performing multi-step manipulation tasks for a Sawyer robot by analyzing three feature categories: speech duration, prosodic expressiveness, and semantic content. By examining these features across four dimensions—demonstration types, audio usage instructions, subtasks, and demonstration styles—the analysis reveals that while duration and expressiveness vary based on the target audience (i.e., the robot's policy), semantic content remains consistent with the subtask regardless of audience or style. Furthermore, when provided with predefined cluster labels, we find that semantic clusters remain stable even when combining demonstrations of identical semantics but differing durations and expressiveness. Consequently, we conclude that audio from human teachers primarily communicates semantic information, with duration and expressiveness serving as stylistic variations. Additionally, this analysis offers a framework for future work in audio-based demonstration characterization. Finally, although the findings are established within a controlled laboratory setting, the emphasized semantic consistency suggests that this approach could be extended to diverse scenarios, such as demonstrations across different human instructors or even dog breeds. The code supporting this analysis is available at: https://github.com/robinfrench/Characterizing_Human_Audio.

We introduce a straightforward framework that utilizes pairwise comparisons to teach robots constraint compliance from natural language audio. This method requires only a subset of comparable constraints and does not rely on hand-crafted features, domain-specific priors, or extensive datasets. To locate comparable constraints, we train a simple classifier to detect semantic features; however, the resulting clusters are not required to align directly with individual constraints. Instead, they serve to guide the robot in navigating the solution space to achieve cluster-level feasibility while adhering to specific individual constraints. The learning algorithm identifies a hyperplane separating feasible and infeasable clusters relative to the robot's solution space, determined by a mix of positive and negative examples from positive constraints and a minority of negative examples from negative constraints. Because this approach does not map constraints to specific features or clusters, it naturally handles abstract concepts like "do not" and efficiently manages both single and multi-constraint scenarios, including those with conflicting requirements. These features are theorized to originate from black hole mergers and evaporation, respectively, from a prior cosmic cycle. We conducted a high-resolution analysis of Planck and WMAP data using "HawkingNet," an open-source machine learning tool built on a ResNet18 architecture designed to detect Hawking points. Our findings indicate that previously reported low-variance circles are artifacts caused by CMB anomalies—specifically, isolated bright pixels that trigger false positives when applying established search criteria. Once these anomalies were excluded, no statistically significant low-variance circles remained. Similarly, no significant evidence for Hawking points was detected using a Gaussian temperature amplitude model with a 1-degree opening angle, particularly after accounting for anomalies. Furthermore, the hypothesis that CMB anomalies themselves are remnants of Hawking points is unsupported, as no surrounding low-variance or high-temperature circles were observed. The lack of these distinct features does not refute the CCC model, as a high density of such circles could instead produce an interference speckle pattern causing non-Gaussian fluctuations, a phenomenon not exclusive to CCC. However, we did identify significant local deviations in the real CMB sky from Gaussian noise on small scales when comparing against best-fit Lambda-CDM and COM PowerSpect CBM TT-full models that incorporate all known small-scale effects. These deviations constitute a novel form of non-Gaussianity not predicted by the standard Lambda-CDM framework, and we argue this actually strengthens the CCC hypothesis, as it aligns with expectations while discrepancies with Lambda-CDM are inevitable. Additionally, significant anti-correlation between the monopole and quadrupole moments in the full sky supports CCC, consistent with the absence of low-variance circles in the opposite hemisphere. We note that the anti-correlation observed in the ecliptic-cut sky is merely a artifact of missing data. Finally, we developed the first all-sky map of likelihoods indicating where low-variance and Hawking circles are located, observing a striking anti-correlation in the placement of these two feature types across the heavens. The paper concludes with a summary of the code used to calculate these likelihoods. As the most rigorous test of CCC to date, this study is unequivocally not a falsification of the model; rather, it is the first to demonstrate that the model must account for certain phenomena. Max-marginal inference provides a robust framework for making decisions within probabilistic models by selecting actions that maximize expected utility. Although essential, executing this process is often computationally demanding, necessitating efficient approximation techniques for practical application. Recently, deep probabilistic models have gained significant attention for their ability to learn complex data distributions and reasoning capabilities. We present a general framework for approximating max-marginal inference within such models. By leveraging recent developments in variational inference and optimal transport, we develop two tractable approaches: the Generalized Mean Field and the Entropic Optimal Transport methods. We demonstrate the versatility of these approaches across various probabilistic models, including factor graphs, normalizing flows, and categorical autoregressive models. Furthermore, we illustrate their applicability to diverse tasks featuring discrete latent variables, such as logical tensor completion, permutation completion, and diverse inference. Experimental results indicate that these methods effectively handle datasets too large for exact max-marginal computation while maintaining competitiveness with established approximation techniques.

It is widely recognized that optimizing a nonconvex function generally yields only local minima. We propose employing oscillatory dynamics to enable an agent to escape these local minima. Specifically, by incorporating a harmonic oscillator, we demonstrate that any dynamic system can be transformed into one exhibiting a "walk and watch" behavior: the agent traverses the state space while monitoring a harmonic component that modulates its movement. Under appropriate conditions, this mechanism facilitates the optimization of nonconvex functions. The term "walk and watch" also finds application in differential game theory to ensure the safety of an opposing player. Consequently, our framework addresses both optimization and safety challenges simultaneously and in a unified manner. To illustrate the approach's effectiveness, we examine two scenarios: an unconstrained nonconvex optimization problem and a constrained differential game. In each case, we show that the method achieves global optimization and maintains the safety property, respectively. The findings indicate that the proposed "walk and watch" mechanism is both powerful and adaptable, applicable to a broad spectrum of dynamic systems.

Deep detectors leverage scene context in distinct ways. This study categorizes object detectors into three groups based on their context utilization: those with no context (RCNN via input cropping), those with partial context (two-stage methods via featuremap cropping), and those with full context (single-stage methods without cropping). We systematically assess the impact of context across these detector categories by constructing a fully controlled dataset with varying contextual conditions and analyzing context usage in deep detectors. Furthermore, we evaluate the effects of progressively removing background and foreground elements on the MS COCO dataset. Our findings indicate that both single-stage and two-stage detectors inherently utilize context through their extensive receptive fields, suggesting that the optimal detector choice often depends on the specific application context. Consequently, future advancements could be achieved by explicitly incorporating context awareness into detector architectures. We release our fully contextualized dataset, "ContextCOCO," which facilitates context evaluation, at https://contextcoco.github.io/. We also provide a detector, "PV-Net," designed with explicit context awareness, demonstrating strong competitive performance. Context evaluation remains a largely unexplored aspect of modern detection systems; however, our results confirm that "PV-Net" outperforms other models on the "ContextCOCO" dataset. The source code for PV-Net and our pretrained weights are available at https://pvnet.detdet.com/.

The study of singularities in the complex plane has historically relied on the concept of the index of a vector field at a singularity. A pivotal result by Hadamard establishes that if a singular point possesses a positive index, the adjacent area must contain other singularities. This paper extends that line of reasoning to the non-smooth setting of Lipschitz vector fields. We demonstrate that a singular point with a positive index for a Lipschitz vector field is necessarily surrounded by other singularities, thereby generalizing the classical theorem. Additionally, we provide several explicit examples of such points with positive index. It should be noted that the primary focus of this research was to advance the study of the Collatz conjecture, which can be framed as a problem in the complex plane; however, a comprehensive exploration of this application is reserved for future work.

Although various methods exist for recommending related entities—ranging from rule-based systems using string similarities like Levenshtein distance to sophisticated approaches relying on external features like DBpedia attributes—the approach described here is fully data-driven. This overview introduces and reviews this extensive category, encompassing elliptical copulas, skew $t$ copulas, factor copulas, time series copulas, and regression copulas. It details the standard auxiliary representation that underpins these models, explaining how this framework ensures scalability and tractability for statistical analysis. Key challenges are examined, including parameter identification, the use of extended likelihoods for discrete or mixed data, maintaining parsimony in high dimensions, and simulation procedures. The text also outlines Bayesian techniques for estimating parameters and generating predictions from implicit copula models. Significant focus is placed on implicit copula processes derived from time series and regression models, which currently represent a leading area of research. Finally, two econometric case studies—one involving macroeconomic time series and the other addressing financial asset pricing—demonstrate the benefits of utilizing implicit copula models. Finally, specific references are provided to expand the framework to marginal models suitable for analyzing count, binary, and other discrete data types. The overarching message is that the implicit copula approach offers an efficient solution for high-dimensional dependence modeling. Following the introduction, the paper outlines its own contributions. Our findings indicate that implicit copulas provide an adaptable framework for studying random vectors and functions across various statistical domains, particularly when parameters are identified via moment matching with theoretical moments based on regression or dependence parameters (Bauer and Mitterecker, 2021). Furthermore, the analysis reveals that many statistical processes defined by non-identifiable joint distributions remain identifiable, and vice versa. While many implicit copula processes allow for efficient maximum likelihood estimation due to non-overidentifiability, this paper highlights that the process itself can be highly robust to minor changes in parameter identification rules, often yielding negligible impacts on posterior parameter estimates. Additionally, we note that many implicit copula processes exhibit ergodic behavior, though the rate of convergence in such cases may be slow. Finally, the process is shown to be applicable for Bayesian prediction, even when parameter estimation from observed data is not feasible. In summary, implicit copulas offer an effective solution for analyzing high-dimensional stochastic processes, whether they are statistically identifiable or not. The issues discussed herein may also extend to other models featuring an auxiliary representation, though those models often lack the same level of versatility found in implicit copula processes. This work provides a theoretical and empirical investigation into the Google News word2vec model. We demonstrate that generative models, such as the n-gram approach, offer a clear framework for constructing objective functions used to compute embeddings. The study examines the Markovian assumption and highlights how n-gram models effectively capture frequentist synonyms while offering a theoretical explanation for the model's limitations in acquiring transitive semantic relations. Empirical analyses are conducted using synthetic corpora and a large-scale collection of financial news articles. The results indicate that wordvec models conflate antonyms, a issue that becomes dynamically non-stationary over time, presenting challenges for their application in machine learning and offering insights into representation learning more broadly. These findings also help explain the observed clustering of words by polarity in recent literature. Ultimately, the discussion offers potential directions for future endeavors, including incorporating morphological information, utilizing transformer-based models, and employing graph neural networks. These elements could help create a objective function that simultaneously captures transitive semantics and transitivity itself.

Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model as the most appropriate choice for the specific setup, demonstrating high accuracy in reproducing LES-derived reaction rate fluctuations. Subsequently, the linearized governing equations, including the linearized EBU model for reaction rates, were solved for incoming acoustic perturbations. The resulting response modes indicate that reaction rate oscillations stem from Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings disturbing the jet flame. These findings align well with LES simulations regarding the mode shapes of both velocity and reaction rate fluctuations. Furthermore, two non-dimensional parameters were defined to estimate the instability thresholds of the flame. The results confirm that these parameters accurately predict the threshold frequencies and growth rates for the computed response modes. Finally, the influences of exit Mach number, turbulent intensity, and stoichiometry on the non-dimensional instability parameters were examined to expand the current understanding of reacting flow stability analysis. This work specifically addresses a turbulent jet flame, highlighting complexities such as those arising from mean shear, turbulence, and density gradients, which are absent in studies of pure fluid jets or constant density flows. The response modes could serve as targets for future experimental investigations, potentially helping to explain observed combustion instabilities in facilities like gas turbines. This approach may also aid in designing experiments to measure reaction rate fluctuations and improve the development of LES closure models. Ultimately, the response modes indicate which parameters are most sensitive to disturbances, which is crucial for optimizing flames. However, it is important to note that the dominant instabilities in many practical scenarios cannot be predicted by a linear analysis alone, necessitating non-linear combustion models. These models are beyond the scope of this work but represent a significant area for future efforts to accurately predict combustion instabilities.

Nonlocal interactions are essential for accurately modeling materials at the microscale and for theoretical extensions of standard physics. Consequently, nonlocal theories have been developed to address material nonlocality and to create analogies between nonlocal electrodynamics and nonlocal gravity. In this study, we examine the implications of a nonlocal constitutive relation within the parameterized post-Newtonian (PPN) formalism. This relation correlates the nonlocal induced stress-energy tensor to the local energy-momentum source. Our analysis demonstrates that nonlocality influences the first post-Newtonian corrections to the PPN parameters. Specifically, the induction current term modifies the gravitational potential, generating a new nonlocal contribution to the metric. This effect becomes particularly relevant near massive bodies. Ultimately, we derive the Schwarzschild solution within this framework.

This approach introduces the significant challenge of resolving conflicts among concurrent updates. Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) offer a principled solution to this problem. To address this, we introduce RWF, the Remove-Win design Framework for CRDTs. Furthermore, performance evaluations of these implementations confirm the efficiency of CRDT designs built upon RWF. CRDTs enable distributed applications to perform in-place updates with high reliability and performance. This paper details the design, implementation, and evaluation of two CRDTs for multi-key value lists, which support multi-key inserts, prefix removes, and removes within the list. These Multi-key Value List CRDTs (MVL-CRDTs) were implemented in Java and integrated into JDT, a modular in-memory distributed application framework. Our evaluations demonstrate that MVL-CRDTs achieve performance comparable to other existing CRDTs for single-key value lists. Additionally, MVL-CRDTs offer several advantages over other available CRDT list designs. Finally, we discuss potential applications for these lists in the context of distributed applications.

A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. Instead, it would be more plausible to suggest that a significant portion of these pulsars has an age of less than a year, meaning they have not yet begun to spin down or have already done so before becoming detectable as pulsars.

The findings from this paper are crucial for comprehensively addressing the issue of mass ejection from such events.

Mirroring classical Coriolis and centrifugal forces, these phenomena include spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and centrifugal redshift. The duration of these effects, which can persist for several picoseconds following excitation, depends on phonon decay rates. As a primary example, we illustrate how to open and close reaction channels in the photodissociation of the Cs₂ molecule. Finally, we propose methods to generate strong spin-dependent forces from vibrational phonons by leveraging quantum interference between multiple molecular modes. Volcanic eruptions release substantial aerosols, notably sulfuric acid, into the atmosphere. These aerosols scatter sunlight, causing skin cancer rates to vary geographically. While latitude and ozone depletion are common factors, we identify a strong local influence of aerosols on cancer rates in specific regions of Japan. Using long-term satellite data on sulfur dioxide (SO₂) concentrations, a proxy for volcanic aerosols, we developed models to estimate these rates. After accounting for latitude, ozone, temperature, and SO₂, the residual analysis reveals that high cancer incidence in areas near active Japanese volcanoes cannot be fully explained by the first three variables alone; the aerosol term is essential for an accurate fit. Furthermore, in certain locations, the correlation shows that lower cancer rates are associated with higher SO₂ levels. We propose that the shade effect of volcanic aerosols reduces sunburns during both day and night periods associated with these eruptions. This mechanism offers a counterintuitive example of localized environmental influences on human health, contrasting with the widely recognized global cooling effect of aerosols.

introduced by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten at the start of the last decade and has rapidly emerged as a central and vibrant field within the representation theory of finite dimensional algebras. These notes serve a dual purpose: first, to provide an accessible introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with a modest background in representation theory, and second, to address the lack of a comprehensive survey by consolidating many of the field's most significant results into a single resource.

Introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory

This section provides a rapid overview of $\tau$-tilting, beginning with foundational definitions and progressing to more advanced concepts.

In their 1979 paper, Morita established that the representation theories of two finite dimensional algebras $A$ and $B$ are equivalent if and only if $A$ is isomorphic to the endomorphism algebra of a faithful finitely generated $B$-module $M$. Later, T. Nakayama made a comparable observation within the framework of Gelfand-Ponomarev theory:

*If $H$ is a non cyclic free product of finite groups, then the representation theories of two $H$-algebras are equivalent if and only if their $H$-finitely generated projective modules are isomorphic.*

While profound, this statement does not fit the $\tau$-tilting framework, as it concerns only projective modules and lacks the nuance found in modern $\tau$-tilting research.

During his young career, I. Reiten frequently collaborated with colleagues to formulate deep results about representation theory using $\tau$-tilting language. A notable example is their work on exceptional collections, which we will explore in a subsequent section.

In 1989, Smith defined a specific class of functors now known as $\tau$-tilting functors. Although this was a significant development, it did not directly lead to $\tau$-tilting theory because, without the concept of $\tau$-tilting modules, these functors could not be fully characterized.

The breakthrough of $\tau$-tilting modules and the subsequent explosion of related research both in Japan and elsewhere can be traced to two parallel discoveries: one by Enomoto, Reiten, and Tachibana, and the other by Iyama and Reiten.

These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. For visual recognition tasks, models are typically trained on extensive datasets. However, in real-world applications, new classes and data streams are constantly introduced, necessitating an incremental learning approach where a model is periodically retrained by adding new classes to the training data. Since released datasets are often incomplete, it is common for new classes to have fewer images than existing ones, making visual recognition from imbalanced data streams a frequent reality. This work examines score calibration methods within an incremental learning framework on imbalanced datasets, highlighting that when updating classes, the resulting model becomes biased toward newly added classes. To mitigate this imbalance, the author proposes various score calibration methods. Furthermore, the author demonstrates that excluding the distillation component from the loss function leads to improved accuracy on benchmark tasks.

When humans or bipedal robots encounter unexpected slipperiness, the typical response is to lower the center of mass (COM) to maintain balance. While prior research has examined the relationship between COM height and slip resistance, it remains unclear how leg configuration influences this stability. This study investigates the standing balance stability of a bipedal support foot relative to its joint angle configurations. Specifically, it analyzes how the foot's resistance to horizontal COM accelerations varies with the angle at the primary support joint—the sole joint capable of actively generating forces to counteract slips. Through mathematical analysis of a simple model and experimental validation using a thruster-assisted bipedal hardware platform, the study demonstrates that the support foot's anti-slip performance reaches local extrema when the primary joint is fully extended or restricted. This finding provides a foundational guideline for designing gait control systems in bipedal robots traversing slippery surfaces.

to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. The study of these distances will be the focus of future research. In classical knot theory, two distinct paths are required to transform any knot into a trivial unknot using the diagonal move. Conversely, for welded knots, the diagonal move functions as an unknotting operation capable of unknottedting any welded knot in a single step. This work also addresses the investigation of singular crossings on classical knot diagrams, which gives rise to the concept of welded knots. Consequently, the classical unknotting distance examined here aligns with the concept of pass moves introduced by Kauffman and Freiling; specifically, the classical unknotting distance via the diagonal move corresponds to the welded crossing change. We establish that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, and all moves belonging to the 4-move family constitute the complete set of welded unknotting operations. Ultimately, the diagonal move represents a more fundamental type of unknotting operation compared to the 4-move. Beyond being an unknotting operation for welded knots, the diagonal move also enables the transformation between two specific quasi-alternating knots. To reach a trivial unknot diagram from either of these quasi-alternating knots using only the diagonal move, a sequence of seven such moves is necessary. Additionally, we establish that these specific quasi-alternating knots represent the maximum possible distance within the diagonal move metric.

Among these, matrix multiplication is the most frequently performed operation; however, it can become computationally expensive when dealing with large datasets. Consequently, parallel computing has emerged as a necessary solution to mitigate this performance bottleneck. This report presents a comparative analysis of sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, implemented using CUDA and OpenMP. Based on collaboration structures, FL is categorized into Horizontal Federated Learning (HFL) and Vertical Federated Learning (VFL). In HFL, entities share identical feature spaces and data samples, whereas in VFL, they share common sample identifiers and collaborate on features. VFL offers a wider application scope and is particularly well-suited for joint model training among large enterprises.

This paper concentrates on VFL, examining potential privacy vulnerabilities within real-world frameworks. We developed and executed two practical privacy attacks: a reverse multiplication attack targeting the logistic regression VFL protocol and a reverse sum attack targeting the XGBoost VFL protocol. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that these attacks are (1) effective, allowing adversaries to extract private training data even when intermediate outputs are encrypted; (2) evasive, as they adhere strictly to protocol specifications and do not degrade the target model's accuracy; and (3) low-effort, requiring minimal prior knowledge of the target participant's data distribution. Furthermore, we show that the information leaked is as potent as the original training data for training alternative classifiers. Finally, we discuss potential countermeasures and their associated challenges, aiming to inspire future research directions.

In horizontal federated learning, participants possess identical feature dimensions but disjoint sample sets, typically exchanging only model parameters under a trusted aggregator's coordination. Conversely, in vertical federated learning, each participant holds a subset of feature dimensions, and the combined feature space across all parties is the Cartesian product of their individual spaces.

We examine two primary privacy risks in VFL: member inference attacks, which aim to reconstruct entire training datasets, and model extraction attacks, which seek to build equivalent local models using leaked intermediate outputs. Recent studies have focused heavily on member inference, leaving intermediate output privacy in under-researched gray areas. This work investigates privacy leaks within intermediate outputs, specifically under the VFL protocol for logistic regression. We demonstrate (1) that an attacker can infer an opponent's private training data from intercepted intermediate outputs; (2) that these attacks do not require access to all local outputs or deviation from the protocol, meaning model performance remains undamaged; and (3) the relatively low knowledge threshold required. Additionally, we propose countermeasures and their limitations. These methods reveal that the attacked party can identify an attacker based on their data distribution, potentially by rejecting outliers, and that the knowledge required is still suboptimal. To overcome this, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, enabling scalability. Despite its popularity, RFF has notable limitations: because it samples features from a distribution independent of the training data, it demands a large number of feature dimensions to match the performance of kernelized classifiers, a requirement that scales with dataset size. Consequently, reducing feature dimensions is essential for effective scaling. This paper introduces Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a data-dependent kernel approximation technique designed to minimize feature dimensions and enhance predictive performance. The method is evaluated on classification and regression tasks, with comparisons made against RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström approach. Empirical results demonstrate that PRFF surpasses these key baselines. Furthermore, due to its low computational cost and minimal memory usage, PRFF is well-suited for integration into broader scalable frameworks such as Iterative Discriminant Analysis. Both classification and regression experiments confirm PRFF's success in predicting low-energy, long-lived 0+ nuclear states from experimental data, outperforming existing kernel approximations. In conclusion, PRFF provides a simple yet powerful solution for scaling kernel methods to large datasets. The code is accessible at https://github.com/Prithvi21/PRFF. In supplementary experiments, we compared PRFF with other random feature approaches, including the Cosine method, and assessed its performance against other kernel approximations on the large-scale MNIST 10-class dataset. These additional findings confirm PRFF's superiority over RFF, orthogonal random features, Nyström, and Cosine features, while also demonstrating that PRFF can be efficiently scaled via low-rank kernel approximation. Finally, we assessed PRFF's performance in a semi-supervised learning context.

fundamental component in object detection systems, yet it has long been observed that its integration often degrades the detection performance of large-scale objects. This paper re-examines FPN within the detection framework to uncover the underlying reasons for its success from an optimization standpoint. We identify that the decline in large-object performance stems from improper back-propagation paths created when FPN is incorporated, which restricts each backbone level to processing objects only within specific scale ranges. Based on this analysis, we propose two viable strategies to ensure every backbone level can perceive objects across all scales in FPN-based architectures. The first strategy involves introducing auxiliary objective functions so that each backbone level directly receives back-propagation signals from objects of various scales during training. The second approach entails constructing the feature pyramid more rationally to eliminate illogical back-propagation routes. Extensive experiments on the COCO benchmark confirm the validity of our analysis and the efficacy of our proposed methods. Without relying on complex additions, we demonstrate that our approach yields substantial improvements (exceeding 2%) across diverse detection frameworks, including one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. Notably, when applied to ResNet-based detectors, our method achieves an unprecedented small-scale object detection mAP of 27.6%. The source code is available at https://github.com/hjy199/All-Scale-Object-Detection.
In the initial phase of object detection utilizing standard Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) designs, the network is trained to identify objects at the lowest pyramid level, which comprises original images, before generating features for subsequent levels. This process implies that the lowest level is the sole component trained to detect objects at the largest scales, while higher levels are back-propagated from the lowest level to capture medium and small objects, respectively. Consequently, the back-propagation pathways become asymmetric and imbalanced, which we contend hinders the performance of large-scale object detection.
We revisit the application of the Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) in object detection to provide a unified, all-scale, pyramid-based architecture where every level is capable of detecting objects across the entire size spectrum. By ensuring that each level can identify both large and small objects, our approach enables the network to detect targets at all scales more effectively and enhances overall detection performance (covering 99.6% of the attention area).

This study focuses on bivariate conditional models that define the distribution of $X$ and the distribution of $Y$ given $X$. Traditional methods for assessing attack effectiveness typically rely on macro-level metrics, like the critical percolation probability ($p_c$) and the size of the giant component, often overlooking the micro-level dynamics of node removals, their specific traits, and immediate outcomes. This paper introduces and applies a micro-scale approach to attack analysis. Grounded in network percolation theory, we examine the "avalanche" effect triggered by the removal of a single node from the giant component—a phenomenon where one removal causes a cascade of disconnections that significantly contributes to network fragmentation and the attack's success beyond the loss of that single node. We specifically analyze the avalanche size, defined as the count of nodes disconnected from the giant component due to one removal. Furthermore, regarding random attacks on Cayley tree networks, we analytically derive the distribution of avalanche sizes throughout the entire attack process, from initiation until the network fully disintegrates. Our findings reveal that avalanche sizes follow a power-law distribution with an exponent of $\delta=2$ for all trees within the giant component below the percolation threshold ($p<p_c$). At the threshold ($p=p_c$), the analysis indicates an infinite avalanche, signifying that a single node removal destroys the entire network. Additionally, we explore the relationships between avalanche size and other attack indicators, such as the number of isolated nodes and the surviving network's node count. These results offer novel insights into the micro-dynamics of network attacks and suggest that avalanche dynamics could serve as a potent tool for evaluating attack efficacy. The findings of this study may also advance the design of optimal attack algorithms and inform general principles for safeguarding networks against attacks. In this context, the critical avalanche exponent could serve as a signature of network attacks and a signature characterizing network topologies. Finally, the study of avalanches finds applications in various other fields, including geophysics, condensed matter physics, and complex systems. Specifically, within the framework of mean-field spin glass theory, we investigate avalanche sizes resulting from changing an external magnetic field. Here, the avalanche size corresponds to the number of spins flipping their direction upon a minor adjustment to the external field. We illustrate the relationship between these sizes and the system's magnetic properties. Within this framework, we uncover the distribution of avalanche sizes for both pure and diluted Cayley tree networks across the entire system evolution. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs).
